One failed SendGrid cancellation prevents deletion of already-cancelled rows

The loop awaits each `client.request` sequentially and only afterwards calls `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)`. If any later SendGrid request throws, the `catch` runs before the delete promises are awaited, so rows for which cancellation already succeeded are not deleted. They remain `cancelled = true` and are retried on the next cron run, generating duplicate SendGrid cancellation requests and keeping stale rows until a run with no cancellation failures. The delete should be awaited immediately after a successful cancellation or the final `Promise.all` should run in a `finally`.

Paid bookings return before scheduled workflow reminders are cancelled

When `bookingToDelete.paid` is true, the handler refunds the payment, marks the booking REJECTED, and returns at this line. This is before the block at lines 484-493 that cancels scheduled workflow reminders. As a result, paid/rejected bookings with scheduled workflow reminders will still have those reminder emails/SMS sent after cancellation. This path is not covered by the PR's cancellation fix.

Request-reschedule workflow reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async and are called in a `forEach` without being awaited. The old code collected and awaited `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` promises. The mutation continues to send the reschedule request and returns; in a serverless environment the process can be frozen before the deferred `cancelled = true` update is written. The old workflow reminders can then still fire after the booking was put into the reschedule path.

Workflow update cancels reminders without awaiting DB writes

`remindersToDelete.flat().forEach(...)` calls the async managers without awaiting them, and the later `userWorkflow.steps.map(async (oldStep) => ...)` promises are also never awaited. The mutation subsequently updates the workflow and returns, so email/SMS cancellation calls and related DB deletes/updates can still be in flight. A cancelled reminder may be re-created or the old reminder may remain uncancelled, allowing emails/SMS from a disabled or edited workflow to be sent after the update completes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach async callbacks are not awaited, so cancellation errors are lost

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` starts an async callback for each reference but `forEach` discards the returned promise. The surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections after the callback suspends, so a failed `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled rejection and the function returns before external calendar/video cancellation is known to have completed. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Recurring cancellation starts unawaited async callbacks and `apiDeletes` is captured too early

In the recurring cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` does not await the callbacks. Each callback suspends at `await getCalendar`, so the later `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` captures `apiDeletes` before these callbacks resume and push their calendar deletions. As a result, recurring calendar events are not deleted/cancelled before booking references and attendees are removed and cancellation emails are sent. Use `await Promise.all(credentials.map(async (credential) => { ... }))` instead of `forEach`.

requestReschedule does not await async calendar/video cancellation callbacks

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` discards the promise returned by each async callback. The mutation continues immediately to send reschedule emails and webhooks, so external calendar/video cancellation for the old booking may still be running, and any rejection from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled rejection. Convert this to `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours validation uses slot start for both start and end

The new working-hours check computes `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` and then `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`, so it never tests slotEndTime. A slot that starts inside the host's work hours but ends after `workingHour.endTime` is not rejected. For round-robin fixed hosts, getTimeSlots can produce such slots from other hosts' longer availability, so fixed hosts can be booked outside their actual working hours.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

false_positives.candidate:
Date override day filter still uses unadjusted organizer wall time

activeOverrides filters overrides by comparing `dayjs.utc(override.start)` with the invitee day. `override.start` is the organizer-local wall time encoded as a UTC timestamp (for example 14:00 IST is stored as T14:00Z), not the actual UTC instant. The new offset conversion later in the function fixes slot minutes but this filter is still applied before that conversion. For attendee timezones whose UTC day differs from the organizer's encoded day, the override can be applied to the previous or next day, so the correct day shows wrong availability.

Date-override slots skip busy checks and can be double-booked

In checkIfIsAvailable, once dateOverrideExist is set and the function has not returned false, it returns true immediately at lines 133-135. This happens before the busy array is checked at line 153. Slots are generated by getTimeSlots without considering busy, so a fixed or loose host with a date override is treated as available even when they have an accepted booking or calendar event during that override. Date overrides should replace normal working hours, not suppress busy checks.

Multiple date overrides on the same day are not all evaluated

The date-override validation uses `dateOverrides.find` and returns true as soon as the slot is outside one same-day override, which makes checkIfIsAvailable return false immediately. If a host has multiple same-day date overrides (for example 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00), a slot in the second override is rejected because the first override does not contain it. Only if no same-day override contains the slot should the slot be considered outside the overridden availability.

No test covers fixed-host date overrides in round-robin events

The new test only exercises a personal event and checks that the returned UTC slots remain the same for a different attendee timezone. The main round-robin fixed-host date-override behavior is untested. A round-robin event with fixed and loose hosts, where the fixed host has a date override, should be added to verify the fix and would have exposed the busy-time and working-hours issues in checkIfIsAvailable.

Split working-hours windows are not all evaluated

The normal working-hours validation similarly uses `workingHours.find` and returns true when a single same-day working-hour window does not contain the slot. A host with split hours (for example 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00) will be treated as unavailable for slots in the later window because the first window is checked first and the function returns false before checking the second. The check should pass if any working-hours window contains the slot, not fail if the first one does not.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing integrations without sender metadata cause KeyError

The check directly accesses integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without guarding for missing or malformed sender data. build_integration only adds metadata['sender'] when state.get('sender') exists, and older integrations or integrations created through paths without sender will not have it. On re-install, GitHubInstallation raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of rendering the installation error page.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub identity is verified by mutable login instead of immutable user id

The pipeline binds only 'login' from get_user_info (lines 434-438) and later compares it to integration.metadata['sender']['login']. GitHub logins are mutable and may be released/reused after a rename, so a different account holding the old login could pass this validation. The sender payload also contains GitHub's immutable user id; compare ids (or at least bind and compare id) to ensure the OAuth-authorized user is actually the installer.

Installation-not-found test no longer reaches the 404 path

The test uses state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', while the pipeline signature in these tests is '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3'. With the new OAuthLoginView, this fails the state check before GitHubInstallation/build_integration runs, so the 404 response configured for /app/installations/{id} is never exercised. The test should use the valid pipeline state to actually cover the 'installation not found' behavior.

OAuth access token exchange omits redirect_uri

The authorization redirect includes redirect_uri (line 408), but the access token request only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub requires the same redirect_uri in the token request whenever it was supplied to /authorize. As written, GitHub will reject the exchange with bad_verification_code or redirect_uri_mismatch, causing real installations to fail. The test stub returns success without checking this parameter, so it is not caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource queued default is evaluated at import time

The dataclass uses `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default. Dataclass defaults are evaluated once when the class is defined, so every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value, including via `from_integration`, gets the module import timestamp rather than the time the assignment source was actually created. Any logic that later reads `queued` for ordering, expiry, or burst detection will see all sources with the same stale timestamp. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing test for propagation to a different integration

The new suppression test only covers an assignment source whose integration matches the outbound target and asserts that outbound sync is not called. There is no test for the other required branch: when an inbound assignment comes from integration A and the group also has a linked issue for integration B, the outbound sync to B should still be scheduled. The same gap exists for inbound deassignment with a matching source. Without this coverage, an over-broad suppression would not be caught.

New should_sync argument can break subclass overrides

The task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with a second positional argument. The base classes were updated to accept this argument, but `should_sync` is a polymorphic method that integrations commonly override with the previous one-argument signature to customize per-direction sync behavior. Any such override now raises `TypeError` on this line, causing assignee-sync tasks to crash instead of running. The same contract concern applies to the new `assignment_source` kwarg passed to `installation.sync_assignee_outbound` for overrides that do not accept `**kwargs`. All existing subclasses/overrides need to be audited and updated, or the call must be made backward-compatible.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated as a detector handler

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` but does not implement the abstract methods `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. It therefore remains an abstract class. `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` references this class, and `Detector.detector_handler` will do `group_type.detector_handler(self)`. For any detector whose type is `metric_alert_fire`, processing will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler ...` instead of evaluating. Either implement the required methods or avoid registering this unsupported handler until it is implemented.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

The docstring on `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` still says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`, but the method now returns a dict keyed by `DetectorGroupKey`. This is misleading for implementers and callers after the signature change.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

false_positives.candidate:
Evaluation crashes for stateful detectors with no counters

`get_state_data` only populates `counter_updates` inside `if self.counter_names:`. When a concrete `StatefulDetectorHandler` defines `counter_names = []` (a valid stateful detector with no Redis counters), `counter_updates` remains `{}`. The `DetectorStateData` construction then accesses `counter_updates[gk]` for each group key and raises `KeyError`, so evaluating any data packet with group values fails. Use `counter_updates.get(gk, {})` or default each group key to `{}`.

Mock occurrence builder ignores `value`, so the new hook's value argument is not verified

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value: int` but never uses it when constructing the expected `IssueOccurrence` or `event_data`. Because expected results in tests such as `test_state_results`, `test_results_on_change`, and `test_dedupe` are built through this helper, those tests would pass even if `evaluate_group_key_value` passed the wrong value to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. The helper should incorporate `value` into the expected occurrence/event data, or tests should assert the hook call received the correct value.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Monitor context returns original config instead of adjusted copy

`get_monitor_environment_context()` creates `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and updates `config["schedule_type"]` to the schedule-type display value, but the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` rather than `config`. The modified copy is never used, so the `schedule_type` display transformation is discarded and the original mutable config is passed into the occurrence context.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Failure threshold can be reached without enough failed check-ins

When `failure_issue_threshold` is greater than 1, the code slices the most recent check-ins to that threshold length and only bails out when one of them is OK. If the monitor environment has fewer than `failure_issue_threshold` check-ins and none is OK (for example, the first check-in of a new monitor fails), `previous_checkins` can contain a single failure, the OK check is false, and the monitor is marked ERROR with an incident created. This defeats the configured consecutive-failure threshold and produces false incidents for new/sparse monitors. The code should require that the window contains the configured number of check-ins or explicitly count consecutive non-OK statuses before creating the incident.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SpanFlusher.join can leave remaining flusher processes running after timeout

When `deadline` is not None and `remaining_time <= 0`, the loop breaks before calling `process.terminate()` on any later processes. Since `self.next_step.join(timeout)` may consume the entire timeout, this commonly skips all flusher processes. If a process is hung and does not observe `self.stopped`, it is never terminated, so old flusher processes can continue flushing and producing Kafka messages after the consumer has moved on. The timeout path should continue terminating all processes even after the deadline expires instead of breaking out of the loop.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Negative --flusher-processes crashes SpanFlusher initialization

The new `--flusher-processes` option is accepted as any int and `SpanFlusher` does not validate that `max_processes` is positive. If a negative value is supplied, `self.num_processes` becomes negative, so `range(self.num_processes)` is empty and `process_to_shards_map` has no keys. The shard distribution loop then computes `process_index = i % self.num_processes` and indexes the empty map, raising `KeyError` and preventing the consumer from starting. Add `click.IntRange(min=1)` or an explicit constructor check.

New flusher_processes parameter inserted before produce_to_pipe breaks positional callers

`ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` now has `flusher_processes` as the sixth positional argument with `produce_to_pipe` seventh. Any existing caller that passed `produce_to_pipe` as the sixth positional argument will now bind that callable to `flusher_processes` and leave `produce_to_pipe` as `None`, silently disabling the pipe/test path or causing type/value errors. `SpanFlusher.__init__` has the same issue with `max_processes`. Prefer keyword-only for the new parameters or append them after existing parameters.

record_stored_segments is called on unused per-flusher buffers

`submit()` now calls `buffer.record_stored_segments()` on each `SpansBuffer` in `self.buffers`. Those buffers are created by `_create_process_for_shards` for the flusher processes and are never passed to `process_batch`/`process_spans`; spans are actually written through the original ingest-side buffer created in `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.create_with_partitions`. The previous code recorded on that ingest-side buffer. Any segment counters or state accumulated by `process_spans` are no longer recorded, so stored-segment metrics can silently underreport or zero out.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Negative max_workers creates an empty queue pool that crashes on submit

`num_queues=max_workers or 20` passes negative values through (e.g. `--max-workers=-1`). FixedQueuePool.__init__ then `range(-1)` creates no queues/workers, and the first `submit` does `self.queues[hash(group_key) % -1]`, which indexes 0 and raises IndexError. Validate `max_workers > 0` or normalize non-positive values.

Shutdown flag can leave queued work unprocessed

OrderedQueueWorker.run checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of the loop. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining queues. If a worker finishes an item and returns to the top while its queue still has items, it exits without calling get() again, so queued WorkItems and their offsets are never processed by this pool. This contradicts the graceful drain implied by `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and can cause in-flight backlog to be dropped until the consumer is restarted. The shutdown flag should not be set before queue drain, or the worker should drain until queue.ShutDown before exiting.

Unbounded per-group queues remove backpressure and can exhaust memory

FixedQueuePool creates `queue.Queue()` without a maxsize, so each per-group queue is unbounded, and FixedQueuePool.submit uses a non-blocking `put`. A single slow subscription will keep all of its messages accumulating in that worker's queue while the main Arroyo loop continues polling and submitting. Contrary to the class docstring's 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', there is no backpressure; memory and OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound, risking OOM and a stalled consumer. Bound the queue or use blocking put with a timeout, and expose pressure metrics/backpressure.

Worker failure still marks offsets complete and commits them

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, exceptions from result_processor are caught and logged, then the finally block at line 149 unconditionally calls complete_offset. The commit loop later commits completed offsets, so a failed result is treated as processed and will not be retried or sent to DLQ. This violates the strategy's stated guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and can silently drop results when result_processor raises. Complete offsets only in the success path; failures should leave the offset outstanding or be explicitly routed to a retry/DLQ path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache test does not prove denial cache is being used

The test `Should deny on explicit cache deny entry` sets the permission cache to `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` and leaves fakeStore permissions empty. If the denial cache lookup were removed or its key did not match, the cached false permission and empty DB result would still produce `Allowed: false`, so the test passes without exercising the denial cache. It should set the cached permission to `true` or provide a DB permission that would allow the request, so the assertion fails if the denial cache is not consulted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key concatenation permits collisions between different resource tuples

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with underscore separators without escaping or length delimiting. These values are not prevented from containing underscores, and an empty parent adds a trailing separator. For example, name=`a_b`, parent=`` produces the same key as name=`a`, parent=`b` for the same user/action. A cached denial for one dashboard/folder can therefore incorrectly deny another resource. Use length-prefixed or hashed components to make the tuple unambiguous.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous denials can deny renderer requests

The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID but not checkReq.IdentityType. Both `anonymous:0` and `render:0` parse to the same userUID `0` in validateSubject, so a denied anonymous Check for a dashboard/folder creates the same permDenialCache key that a later renderer Check for the same namespace/action/name/folder will hit. The renderer path would normally return allowed for `dashboards:read` via getRendererPermissions, but the cached denial is returned first. An attacker who can cause repeated anonymous denied checks can keep this entry warm and deny rendering for that resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem is rendered without a React key

In `FilterViewResults`, `rules.map` destructures `key` from each `RuleWithOrigin`, and the datasource and unknown branches pass `key={key}` to their list items. The `grafana` branch returns `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` without a key. React will warn and may reuse or misreconcile component state when Grafana rules are reordered, added, or removed. Add `key={key}` to this branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is shown but clicking it does nothing when only promRule is available

In the new prom-only rule list, RuleActionsButtons receives no `rule`/rulerRule. AlertRuleMenu shows the Silence item because `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` can report it as supported and allowed, and clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true. However this render condition requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`; with `rule` undefined it is false, so `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` is never rendered and the user-visible action is a dead click. Either hide/disable the Silence item when no ruler rule is available or make the drawer work from the prom rule.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete action is hidden for prom-only Grafana rules even when canDelete is true

The new alert list view passes `promRule` but no `rulerRule`. `canDelete` can be true via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, but the Delete menu item is guarded by both `canDelete` and `rulerRule`. Since `rulerRule` is undefined in the prom-only list, users with delete permission no longer see Delete for Grafana rules. `RuleActionsButtons` already builds a valid identifier from `promRule`, so this guard should be updated or the removal should be intentional and documented.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable in CombinedRule ability checks

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (still used by `useAlertRuleAbility` and `useAlertRuleAbilities`) now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false`. The previous `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` implementation computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and used it to make Update, Delete, Pause, and Restore unsupported for federated rule groups. After this change, CombinedRule callers can report those actions as supported for federated rules when the user has ordinary permissions, so the UI may expose edit/delete actions that are disallowed for federated rules.

Pause action is never shown for prom-only Grafana rules despite canPause

`canPause` is computed using either rulerRule or Grafana prom rule abilities, and can be true in the new prom-only list. However the Pause menu item is additionally guarded by `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. With no rulerRule, the Pause item never renders, so the newly added `grafanaPauseAbility` is ineffective and pause access disappears from the alert list view.

Rule view link no longer preserves returnTo navigation

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` implementation used `createReturnTo()` and passed `{ returnTo }` to `createRelativeUrl` when building the rule view href. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` builds the same href without `returnTo`, so navigating from the rule list to the rule view no longer carries the return location and in-app back/return behavior can be regressed. If this is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise the `returnTo` query should be retained.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting bypasses the $__range split guard

The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` runs before `querySupportsSplitting`. `querySupportsSplitting` is designed to reject queries containing `$__range`/`$__range_ms` via `isQueryWithRangeVariable`, with a comment explaining these queries must not be split because the range variable would be interpreted relative to the split sub-range and produce an incorrect result. Since `applyTemplateVariables` replaces `$__range`/`$__range_ms`, the check on the interpolated expr no longer sees them and will allow time-splitting of those queries. The range-variable check should be performed on the pre-interpolated expression or otherwise preserve the raw expression for this guard.

Queries can become empty after interpolation but are not re-filtered

The target pipe filters `query.expr` before `applyTemplateVariables`. When a non-empty template expression such as `$var` resolves to an empty string, the query remains in `queries` and proceeds through partitioning. Since the interpolated empty expr is not a logs query, it is treated as a metric query and sent to Loki with `expr: ''`. Reorder the pipe to interpolate first and then `.filter((query) => query.expr)` so queries whose value is empty are skipped.

Shard splitting applies template variables twice per query

`runShardSplitQuery` now interpolates every target with `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` at line 52. Later, `splitQueriesByStreamShard` sends each shard sub-request through `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which now also applies `applyTemplateVariables` to each target. Each query is interpolated again for every shard/time sub-request; the test change even asserts `applyTemplateVariables` is called five times for a single target. If variable replacement is not idempotent (for example, a variable value contains `$` or template-variable syntax), the second pass can change the query incorrectly. One of the two layers should avoid re-interpolating already-interpolated targets.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request logs lose traceID

The previous `logRequest` appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to the request completion log. This change removes that field and the `tracing` import. The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname; it does not add a trace ID. Unless some unchanged middleware already injects traceID as a contextual log attribute, `Plugin Request Completed` entries will no longer contain a trace ID, breaking log-to-trace correlation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext drops the logger whose logs tests inspect

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning `f` or a logger that shares `f`'s `Logs` fields. Since `LoggerMiddleware` now logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, any test that passes a `*TestLogger` and then asserts on the original logger's `InfoLogs`/`ErrorLogs` will observe zero calls because the actual log is written to a brand-new `TestLogger`. The fake should preserve the same test logger or share its log counters/fields.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to Logger is a source-breaking interface change

The exported `log.Logger` interface now requires `FromContext(context.Context) Logger`. Any existing implementation outside this package, including external/enterprise code, will no longer satisfy the interface and will fail to compile until it adds the method. If `pkg/plugins/log` is consumed as an API, this should be introduced as an optional interface or with a compatibility/deprecation path.

Exported InstrumentationMiddleware symbols removed without compatibility aliases

This renames the exported `InstrumentationMiddleware` type and `NewInstrumentationMiddleware` constructor to `MetricsMiddleware` and `NewMetricsMiddleware`. Because `pkg/services/pluginsintegration/clientmiddleware` is not an `internal` package, downstream importers such as enterprise or external code will fail to compile after upgrading. If the package is public API, keep deprecated alias symbols during the transition or coordinate the breaking change explicitly.

LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware

`LoggerMiddleware` no longer includes pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, or dsUID in its own log params. It now calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` and expects those fields to already be present in the context. Production middleware ordering in `CreateMiddlewares` inserts `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` before it, so the production path gets those fields. However `NewLoggerMiddleware` is exported and can be used independently; any caller that builds a middleware stack without the new contextual middleware will get request logs with those fields silently missing. This hidden ordering dependency should be documented, enforced, or avoided by keeping the fields inside `LoggerMiddleware`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, performs an upsert. There is no transaction, lock, or database-enforced cap around these two operations. Concurrent requests from different devices can all observe a count below the limit and then insert, so the configured device limit can be exceeded under normal concurrent anonymous traffic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit rejection is bypassable by retrying with the same device ID

In tagDeviceUI the local cache entry is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice. When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry remains. TagDevice propagates the error so the first anonymous authentication request fails, but any subsequent request with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id on the same instance within the 29-minute local-cache TTL sees the cached key and returns nil without touching the store. Anonymous.Authenticate then succeeds, so a client can bypass the configured device limit simply by retrying.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication now blocks on synchronous device-store writes

Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously before returning an identity. On a local-cache miss, TagDevice performs a database count when the limit is enabled and an insert/update upsert for each new device, and again after the 29-minute local-cache TTL. Previously this work ran in a background goroutine with a timeout and did not delay login. This adds database latency and database-availability risk to the anonymous authentication path.

Authn client is coupled to the anonstore storage package for a sentinel error

Authenticate imports pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore and uses errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached). This couples the authentication client to a concrete database-store implementation. The sentinel error should be part of the anonymous service contract or a shared service package so alternate anonymous.Service implementations can signal the same condition without importing storage internals.

Clients can bypass the device limit by omitting the device ID header

TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is empty. Since Anonymous.Authenticate now only rejects when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, an anonymous request that omits this header is never counted and always proceeds even when the configured limit has been reached. If the device limit is intended to be enforced, missing or empty device IDs should not silently skip enforcement.

RowsAffected == 0 can incorrectly reject existing devices on MySQL

updateDevice treats RowsAffected() == 0 as proof that no existing device was updated and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL default behavior, the affected-row count for UPDATE is the number of rows changed, not rows matched. An existing device row whose client_ip, user_agent, and updated_at already equal the supplied values can produce 0 affected rows and be rejected incorrectly. Use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS, a follow-up existence check, or otherwise distinguish 'updated an existing row' from 'no matching row'.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup logs successful batch operations at error level

The new batch cleanup code calls r.log.Error for every batch even when there is no error: see lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579. For example, after fetchIDs succeeds, line 534 logs 'Annotations to clean by time' with err=nil, and line 537 logs 'cleaned annotations by time' even when deleteByIDs returns nil. These calls happen for no-op batches with zero IDs and can include large 'ids' slices up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (e.g. 32767). This floods logs with error-level events during normal cleanup, can trigger log-based alerts, and is misleading. Use Debug/Info for successful batch progress and avoid logging full ID slices at Error level.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The ticker interval for the entire cleanup service was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and greatly increases how often all cleanup jobs run, including snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history. Since clean() has a 9-minute timeout and cleanup jobs can take a while, a 1-minute ticker can cause cleanup to run nearly continuously or back-to-back. If this was not intentional, it should be reverted or explicitly justified.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded with the storage metric

The async legacy `DeleteCollection` result is recorded with `recordStorageDuration` and `startLegacy`. It should use `recordLegacyDuration`. As written, legacy successes and failures are attributed to storage metrics, corrupting both metric sets.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name as the metric kind label

This line passes `name` as the kind argument to `recordStorageDuration`, while other calls pass `options.Kind`. `name` is a user-controlled object name, so every deleted object creates a new Prometheus label value. This causes unbounded cardinality in the mode 3 storage metrics and can make metrics expensive or unusable. It should pass `options.Kind`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled after return

The goroutine at this line wraps the incoming request context with a 10s timeout and then performs Legacy.Create. The same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 108, 134, 161). In Kubernetes API server storage, the context passed to the storage method is typically canceled when the HTTP handler returns. Since this method returns immediately after launching the goroutine, the legacy backup write frequently starts with an already canceled context and is aborted, so mode 3 does not reliably keep legacy storage as a safe backup. Detach from the request lifecycle, for example with context.WithoutCancel/context.Background, before applying the timeout.

Legacy update reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object written to unified storage

This line passes the same `objInfo` that was already consumed by `d.Storage.Update` to `d.Legacy.Update`. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` may be single-use or may compute the new object against the old object in the target store; because legacy may have a different old object than unified storage, legacy can produce a different object or fail. The previous implementation wrapped the final object returned by storage in `updateWrapper` for the legacy update. The async legacy update should use the object returned by `d.Storage.Update`, or a wrapper that returns that object, rather than the original `objInfo`.

Mode 3 integration tests immediately assert legacy consistency despite async legacy writes

The new mode 3 subtests run `doPlaylistTests`, which after k8s Create/Update immediately calls the legacy API and asserts that the change is present (for example the legacy list check and `getFromBothAPIs`). Mode 3 now writes to legacy asynchronously after the unified storage write returns, so these checks race with the legacy-write goroutine and can fail intermittently in CI. The tests should poll or wait for legacy convergence, or use a mode-specific expectation for async propagation.

Storage create/update errors are recorded as legacy durations

On a `Storage.Create` error, the code records `recordLegacyDuration` with the storage start time even though no legacy call was made. The same mistake is present in `Update` at line 129. These should be `recordStorageDuration`. As written, storage failure metrics are underreported and legacy duration metrics are polluted with storage call durations.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing cache re-check after acquiring write lock causes thundering herd and I/O under exclusive lock

After the initial RLock sees entryPointAssetsCache == nil, the function takes the write lock and immediately performs readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN without re-reading entryPointAssetsCache. Multiple goroutines that all observed nil will therefore serialize on the write lock and each recompute and overwrite the cache, while all other GetWebAssets callers are blocked. Add a second check for a non-nil cache after acquiring the write lock (or use singleflight) before doing I/O.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent test for the race fix

The PR changes shared-state synchronization but adds no test that exercises GetWebAssets concurrently. A test invoking GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines (run under the race detector) would verify both that the cache assignment is race-free and that the cache population path behaves correctly under contention.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, making the sqlExpressions toggle a no-op

The function reads `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, but both control-flow branches return false, so SQL expressions are rejected regardless of whether the feature toggle is enabled. This makes the still-existing `sqlExpressions` feature flag a no-op and leaves the `QueryTypeSQL` parsing branch below unreachable. If disabling is intentional, it should be explicit (for example `return false` with a comment), or the toggle/docs should be updated; otherwise the dead flag and unreachable code create a misleading contract and a future risk of accidental re-enable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test covers that SQL expressions are disabled

The PR changes behavior for all SQL expression queries but includes no tests asserting the new rejection behavior. There should be a regression test for `ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` returning an error, and for `NewSQLCommand`/`UnmarshalSQLCommand` rejecting SQL commands without doing any DuckDB work, so this security fix cannot be accidentally reverted by future refactors.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fine-grained BuildIndex lock permits concurrent builds for the same key

BuildIndex now takes cacheMu only when inserting into b.cache. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go is not singleflight: callers can both call GetIndex, see nil, and call build concurrently. For file-backed indexes both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory at the same time, which can fail or corrupt the index; even for memory indexes, the later insertion can overwrite a fresher index. Re-check the cache after acquiring cacheMu or add per-key singleflight before building.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race in init errgroup goroutines

The goroutines launched by group.Go all execute totalBatchesIndexed++ and _, _, err = s.build(...) using variables captured from the enclosing function. These are unsynchronized concurrent writes to the same variables (and err is returned), so this is a data race: increments can be lost and error propagation is undefined. Use local variables in the closure and an atomic counter, or update metrics after group.Wait.

Error path leaks the server context and started services

NewResourceServer creates a cancelable ctx for the server's background work and then calls s.Init(ctx). If Init fails, it returns nil, err without calling s.cancel() or stopping the lifecycle. Since the server is not returned, the caller cannot call Stop. By that point search.init may already have started its watch goroutine, and Init may have initialized the backend, so these resources leak. Cancel ctx and perform cleanup on this path.

Ignored build resource version causes permanent index gaps

s.build returns the last RV consumed from ListIterator, and the call in init discards it. After all builds, init starts WatchWriteEvents, but the SQL implementation starts from the latest RV at that moment and has no since parameter. Writes that land after a resource's ListIterator scan and before WatchWriteEvents starts are neither in the built index nor replayed, so the index can remain stale at least until restart or reindex.

Postgres integration test skipped

This change disables the storage-server integration test for postgres due to CI failures. That leaves the postgres unified-storage path without this integration coverage and may hide regressions in the new eager-init behavior. Either fix the underlying failure or file and track a concrete issue rather than silently skipping.

Watch goroutine panics on closed channel

The search watcher loop reads v := <-events without checking ok or selecting on a done context. When the backend closes the event stream during shutdown, v is a nil *WrittenEvent and handleEvent immediately dereferences evt.Type, causing an unrecovered panic. It also uses context.Background() rather than a cancelable context, so it cannot be stopped cleanly. Check the ok value and return on channel close, and use a cancellable context.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers the wrong alias for created identity providers

Line 381 (and similarly line 425) uses testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove instead of the actual idpRep.getAlias(). As a result, the created idp-alias-* identity providers are not removed during cleanup, and remain in the realm for later tests or reruns. This can cause cross-test pollution or duplicate-alias failures, and may also remove an unrelated IdP that actually has the alias 'alias'.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache invalidation misses realm-level IdP BROKER_PUBLIC changes

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate returns without invalidating when both old and new models pass getLoginPredicate() and have the same organizationId. For a realm-level IdP (organizationId == null), getLoginPredicate() is true regardless of OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC. However getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, null) populates its cache from a delegate query that searches BROKER_PUBLIC=true without requiring an organization link, so a realm-level IdP with BROKER_PUBLIC=true can be part of that cached result. Changing BROKER_PUBLIC on such an already login-eligible realm-level IdP therefore does not invalidate the ORG_ONLY cache, leaving a stale broker list on the login page until some other login-relevant mutation invalidates it.

remove() can leave a stale getById cache entry on alias cache miss

When isInvalid(cacheKey) is false and the alias cache entry is null, the removal path does not call registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp). If the IdP was previously loaded by internal id (cached under that id) but its alias key was never cached or was evicted, idpDelegate.remove(alias) deletes the entity while the internal-id cache entry remains. A subsequent getById(internalId) then returns the deleted IdP. Since storedIdp is now loaded unconditionally at line 100, it should be invalidated in all removal paths.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider, not BouncyCastle

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() documents that it returns a BouncyCastle security provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is typically the JDK SUN/SunJSSE provider when BC is not present. Any caller that relies on the returned provider being BC, for BC algorithms or provider-specific registration, gets the wrong provider, which can lead to algorithm lookup failures or inconsistent provider behavior. The provider should return the actual BC provider it uses, or null if it intentionally does not use BC, with callers updated accordingly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public interface. Adding an abstract int order() method without a default implementation breaks both source and binary compatibility for any third-party or otherwise out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider; such implementations will fail to compile or will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime. The method should have a default implementation, for example returning a neutral order, unless this is a deliberately accepted breaking API change.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA conversion test uses one default EC key for all curves and only tests round-trip

The test generates a single KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() without specifying a curve. For ES384 and ES512 the key is not necessarily on P-384 or P-521, and the test only asserts that DER -> R||S -> DER equals the intermediate R||S. It does not verify the conversions against the JCA signature value or against known test vectors, so an incorrect implementation could pass while producing wrong encodings for the actual algorithm or curve. Use per-algorithm curve parameters and assert the expected raw signature/conversion result.

Registered crypto provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for core crypto operations

AuthzClientCryptoProvider is advertised through META-INF/services and will be auto-selected when no higher-order provider is present. Yet getSignature(), getKeyPairGen(), getKeyFactory(), getCertificateUtils(), getPemUtils(), and most other CryptoProvider methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. Standalone authz-client code that uses these SPI methods, such as JWT client authentication or other signature operations via CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getSignature(...), will fail at runtime instead of using the JCA defaults. Either implement the needed methods using standard JCA or do not register a class as a general CryptoProvider until it is complete.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client deletion cleanup is gated on the old FGAP feature and has no V2 path

registerListener now wraps role/client/group cleanup in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), but the factory methods in the same class choose MgmtPermissionsV2 based on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. When only V2 is enabled, ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent is ignored, so authorization resources created for a deleted client are never removed. If both flags are enabled, management(...).clients() resolves to ClientPermissionsV2 and setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean) throws UnsupportedOperationException, so client deletion breaks. Client cleanup needs a V2 implementation rather than being gated on the V1 feature flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission cannot return per-client resources

getClientsWithPermission iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...), but per-client resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource are created with resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId()) and never have their type set to CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE. Only the type-level resource named "Clients" has that type. As a result, the method misses all concrete client resources and may return the pseudo-resource "Clients" when a type-level permission exists. Callers that treat the returned set as client IDs will either see no concrete clients or an invalid ID.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
All-client permission is skipped once a per-client resource exists

hasPermission(ClientModel, String) evaluates the all-clients resource only when no resource exists for that client. If any per-client resource exists, for example a VIEW or CONFIGURE permission for that client, the type-level Clients resource is not evaluated. The per-client checks canManage(ClientModel), canConfigure(ClientModel), canMapRoles(ClientModel), canMapCompositeRoles(ClientModel), and canMapClientScopeRoles(ClientModel) all rely on this method, so a caller with a valid MANAGE/CONFIGURE/MAP_ROLES permission for all clients can be denied for any client that also has some individual permission. Conversely, a negative type-level Clients policy is not considered for such clients, which can allow an action that the all-clients policy was intended to deny. The all-clients resource should always be evaluated together with any individual client resource.

Test mutates shared client name without cleanup

testManageOnlyOneClient changes myclient's clientId/name to "somethingNew" via clientResource.update(myclient) and never restores it. Other tests in the same class, such as testConfigureOnlyOneClient and testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient, look up clients with realm.admin().clients().findByClientId("myclient").get(0). If this test runs before them, those lookups return an empty list and the tests fail. Restore the client in a finally block or @AfterEach, or avoid changing the shared fixture.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Public exit code meaning changed from 4 to 3

`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` was changed from 4 to 3, and 4 now means the `rolling-updates` feature is disabled. This is a user-visible contract change for any scripts already written against the previous preview behavior, especially because the accompanying documentation tells users to rely on the exit code. If backward compatibility matters for preview users, this should be called out or a non-conflicting new code should be used.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Feature-disabled exit code and check subcommand are not tested

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only exercises the `metadata` subcommand and asserts the error text, but does not assert the newly documented exit code 4 for the feature-disabled case. The `check` subcommand has an identical feature gate that is not covered in this test. A regression in the exit code or in `UpdateCompatibilityCheck`'s feature gate would not be caught.

Operator feature requirement is stated unconditionally but default update behavior does not enable it

The caution says the Operator will fail unless `rolling-updates` is enabled, with no qualification. However, `UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment` only enables the feature when an explicit `UpdateStrategy` is configured; the default/null strategy test cases exercise operator update behavior without it and are expected to succeed. This either overstates the requirement and will lead users to enable a preview feature unnecessarily, or the tests are not covering a real failure in the default path.

Recreate exit code is not asserted

The wrong-version tests assert the printed error messages but never assert that the command exits with `CompatibilityResult.RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` (now 3). The exit code is the documented contract for automation, and its value was changed in this PR, so the tests should verify it rather than relying only on output text.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group view permission incorrectly grants manage/create access

`canManage()` returns true when the caller has either `VIEW` or `MANAGE` on the all-groups resource (`hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`). `requireManage()` is used by `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` before creating a top-level group, so a principal granted only view access to all groups can create groups. It should require only `MANAGE`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses authorization resource ID instead of group ID

`getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` passes `groupResource.getId()` to `hasPermission(...)`, but `hasPermission` starts with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`. In `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` the resource name is the actual group ID, while `groupResource.getId()` is the internal authorization resource UUID. It also adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set. User search puts those IDs into `UserModel.GROUPS`, so the membership filter is wrong and can return no users for group view-members/manage-members permissions. It should use `groupResource.getName()` and add `groupResource.getName()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Individually created group resources are not assigned the Groups type

When `getOrCreateResource` creates a new resource for a group, it calls `resourceStore.create(...)` and updates scopes but never calls `resource.setType(resourceType)`. `GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` discovers group resources with `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)`, so these individual group resources will not be found; only the aggregate all-groups resource created in `init` has the type. This breaks group-membership-based user search filtering.

Per-group authorization evaluation replaced one global short-circuit

The new code filters with `stream.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)` instead of evaluating `groupsEvaluator.canView()` once and short-circuiting. For callers with fine-grained all-groups view/manage but no legacy admin role, `canView(group)` performs a resource lookup and policy evaluation for every group. On realms with many groups this makes the group listing endpoint significantly more expensive. The same pattern was removed in `GroupResource.getSubGroups`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian account message replaced with Italian text

The new totpStep1 value is 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian, while this is a Lithuanian resource file. Lithuanian users will see Italian text in the OTP setup instructions instead of the translated instruction.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified Chinese account message replaced with Traditional Chinese text

The new totpStep1 value '在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：' uses Traditional Chinese characters (手機, 應用程式), but this is the Simplified Chinese locale file. Simplified Chinese users will see Traditional Chinese text mixed into the otherwise Simplified Chinese UI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Diff substring can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when prefix and suffix overlap

The common-prefix/common-suffix loop computes start and end independently. If the sanitized and original values differ only in a middle region and the common suffix overlaps the common prefix (for example with repeated or symmetric text), end can become greater than length - start, so value.substring(start, value.length() - end) is called with an end index before the start index. This throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException and crashes the Maven verifier instead of reporting the actual 'Illegal HTML' difference.

Lithuanian login message replaced with Italian text

The new loginTotpStep1 value is 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian, while this is a Lithuanian resource file. Lithuanian users will see Italian text in the OTP setup instructions instead of the translated instruction.

PropertyResourceBundle is loaded with ISO-8859-1 instead of UTF-8

PropertyResourceBundle created from FileInputStream uses Properties.load(InputStream), which decodes bytes as ISO-8859-1. The Keycloak message properties are UTF-8 and contain raw non-Latin scripts such as Chinese, Arabic, and Cyrillic. Both the target and English bundles are therefore decoded to mojibake before sanitization and before any violation text is generated. Use a Reader with UTF-8 (for example Files.newBufferedReader) for both bundles so verification and error messages operate on the real message text.

i18next placeholders and ICU choice will render literally in React admin/account UIs

This file is consumed by the React account UI, where interpolation uses the i18next syntax {{0}}, {{1}}, etc. (see all other keys in this file such as backTo=Back to {{app}}). The new value uses Java MessageFormat placeholders {0}, {1} and a {2,choice,...} segment. i18next will not interpolate those or evaluate the choice format, so users will see literal braces and format text instead of the actual counted value. The same addition was made in js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources/theme/keycloak.v2/admin/messages/messages_en.properties.

This contradicts the graceful drain implied by `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and can cause in-flight backlog to be dropped until the consumer is restarted. Multiple goroutines that all observed nil will therefore serialize on the write lock and each recompute and overwrite the cache, while all other GetWebAssets callers are blocked. This causes unbounded cardinality in the mode 3 storage metrics and can make metrics expensive or unusable. It should pass `options.Kind`.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled after return

The goroutine at this line wraps the incoming request context with a 10s timeout and then performs Legacy.Create. The same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 108, 134, 161). In Kubernetes API server storage, the context passed to the storage method is typically canceled when the HTTP handler returns. Since this method returns immediately after launching the goroutine, the legacy backup write frequently starts with an already canceled context and is aborted, so mode 3 does not reliably keep legacy storage as a safe backup. Detach from the request lifecycle, for example with context.WithoutCancel/context.Background, before applying the timeout.

Legacy update reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object written to unified storage

This line passes the same `objInfo` that was already consumed by `d.Storage.Update` to `d.Legacy.Update`. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` may be single-use or may compute the new object against the old object in the target store; because legacy may have a different old object than unified storage, legacy can produce a different object or fail. The previous implementation wrapped the final object returned by storage in `updateWrapper` for the legacy update. The async legacy update should use the object returned by `d.Storage.Update`, or a wrapper that returns that object, rather than the original `objInfo`.

Storage create/update errors are recorded as legacy durations

On a `Storage.Create` error, the code records `recordLegacyDuration` with the storage start time even though no legacy call was made. The same mistake is present in `Update` at line 129. These should be `recordStorageDuration`. As written, storage failure metrics are underreported and legacy duration metrics are polluted with storage call durations.

Legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded with the storage metric

The async legacy `DeleteCollection` result is recorded with `recordStorageDuration` and `startLegacy`. It should use `recordLegacyDuration`. As written, legacy successes and failures are attributed to storage metrics, corrupting both metric sets.

Mode 3 integration tests immediately assert legacy consistency despite async legacy writes

The new mode 3 subtests run `doPlaylistTests`, which after k8s Create/Update immediately calls the legacy API and asserts that the change is present (for example the legacy list check and `getFromBothAPIs`). Mode 3 now writes to legacy asynchronously after the unified storage write returns, so these checks race with the legacy-write goroutine and can fail intermittently in CI. The tests should poll or wait for legacy convergence, or use a mode-specific expectation for async propagation.

The previous `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` implementation computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and used it to make Update, Delete, Pause, and Restore unsupported for federated rule groups. After this change, CombinedRule callers can report those actions as supported for federated rules when the user has ordinary permissions, so the UI may expose edit/delete actions that are disallowed for federated rules.

The new alert list view passes `promRule` but no `rulerRule`. `canDelete` can be true via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, but the Delete menu item is guarded by both `canDelete` and `rulerRule`.
