`canPause` is computed using either rulerRule or Grafana prom rule abilities, and can be true in the new prom-only list. However the Pause menu item is additionally guarded by `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. With no rulerRule, the Pause item never renders, so the newly added `grafanaPauseAbility` is ineffective and pause access disappears from the alert list view.

Rule view link no longer preserves returnTo navigation

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` implementation used `createReturnTo()` and passed `{ returnTo }` to `createRelativeUrl` when building the rule view href. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` builds the same href without `returnTo`, so navigating from the rule list to the rule view no longer carries the return location and in-app back/return behavior can be regressed. If this is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise the `returnTo` query should be retained.

Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting bypasses the $__range split guard

The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` runs before `querySupportsSplitting`. `querySupportsSplitting` is designed to reject queries containing `$__range`/`$__range_ms` via `isQueryWithRangeVariable`, with a comment explaining these queries must not be split because the range variable would be interpreted relative to the split sub-range and produce an incorrect result. Since `applyTemplateVariables` replaces `$__range`/`$__range_ms`, the check on the interpolated expr no longer sees them and will allow time-splitting of those queries. The range-variable check should be performed on the pre-interpolated expression or otherwise preserve the raw expression for this guard.

`runShardSplitQuery` now interpolates every target with `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` at line 52. Later, `splitQueriesByStreamShard` sends each shard sub-request through `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which now also applies `applyTemplateVariables` to each target. Each query is interpolated again for every shard/time sub-request; the test change even asserts `applyTemplateVariables` is called five times for a single target. If variable replacement is not idempotent (for example, a variable value contains `$` or template-variable syntax), the second pass can change the query incorrectly. One of the two layers should avoid re-interpolating already-interpolated targets.

Queries can become empty after interpolation but are not re-filtered

The target pipe filters `query.expr` before `applyTemplateVariables`. When a non-empty template expression such as `$var` resolves to an empty string, the query remains in `queries` and proceeds through partitioning. Since the interpolated empty expr is not a logs query, it is treated as a metric query and sent to Loki with `expr: ''`. Reorder the pipe to interpolate first and then `.filter((query) => query.expr)` so queries whose value is empty are skipped.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, performs an upsert. There is no transaction, lock, or database-enforced cap around these two operations. Concurrent requests from different devices can all observe a count below the limit and then insert, so the configured device limit can be exceeded under normal concurrent anonymous traffic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: the device count check and insertion are not atomic, allowing concurrent requests to exceed the device limit. Both suggest transaction or locking protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit rejection is bypassable by retrying with the same device ID

In tagDeviceUI the local cache entry is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice. When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry remains. TagDevice propagates the error so the first anonymous authentication request fails, but any subsequent request with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id on the same instance within the 29-minute local-cache TTL sees the cached key and returns nil without touching the store. Anonymous.Authenticate then succeeds, so a client can bypass the configured device limit simply by retrying.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same cache-ordering bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice, leaves it cached after ErrDeviceLimitReached, and lets subsequent requests bypass the device limit during the 29-minute cache TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
Clients can bypass the device limit by omitting the device ID header

TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is empty. Since Anonymous.Authenticate now only rejects when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, an anonymous request that omits this header is never counted and always proceeds even when the configured limit has been reached. If the device limit is intended to be enforced, missing or empty device IDs should not silently skip enforcement.

Anonymous authentication now blocks on synchronous device-store writes

Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously before returning an identity. On a local-cache miss, TagDevice performs a database count when the limit is enabled and an insert/update upsert for each new device, and again after the 29-minute local-cache TTL. Previously this work ran in a background goroutine with a timeout and did not delay login. This adds database latency and database-availability risk to the anonymous authentication path.

RowsAffected == 0 can incorrectly reject existing devices on MySQL

updateDevice treats RowsAffected() == 0 as proof that no existing device was updated and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL default behavior, the affected-row count for UPDATE is the number of rows changed, not rows matched. An existing device row whose client_ip, user_agent, and updated_at already equal the supplied values can produce 0 affected rows and be rejected incorrectly. Use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS, a follow-up existence check, or otherwise distinguish 'updated an existing row' from 'no matching row'.

Authn client is coupled to the anonstore storage package for a sentinel error

Authenticate imports pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore and uses errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached). This couples the authentication client to a concrete database-store implementation. The sentinel error should be part of the anonymous service contract or a shared service package so alternate anonymous.Service implementations can signal the same condition without importing storage internals.

The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only called from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. `I18n.translate` in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb` lazy-loads only the current locale via `load_locale(config.locale)`, so translations performed outside controller actions (for example mailers, background jobs, or rake tasks) with a non-default locale will not have the site-default or `:en` YAML loaded before fallback lookup runs. A missing key in the current locale can then fail or produce an I18n missing-translation error instead of falling back. The fallback preloading must happen wherever `I18n.locale` is set, or `translate` should load the fallback chain itself.

Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain

The cached translation key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. With the new fallback chain `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]`, a translation that is missing in the requested locale can be resolved from a fallback locale and then cached under the requested locale. If `SiteSetting.default_locale` changes at runtime, the same key and locale would need a different fallback resolution, but the old cached value is still returned until `I18n.reload!` clears the cache. This can serve stale translations after an admin changes the default locale. Include the fallback chain in the cache key or invalidate the translation cache when the default locale changes.

No tests cover the new fallback behavior

This PR introduces a custom fallback order, loads fallbacks and pluralization in a new initializer, removes environment-specific fallback flags, and adds `ensure_loaded!` wiring, but no specs are added. The behavior should be tested: anonymous users use the site default, logged-in users fall back in the expected order, fallback locale YAMLs are actually loaded, and non-controller translation paths do not regress. Without tests, this lazy-loading/fallback interaction is easy to break.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `fetch` to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body. There is no secret, signature, or API key. Anyone who can reach the sync endpoint can request access tokens for arbitrary Cal.com user IDs. Since this endpoint returns third-party credentials, add an authenticated header/shared secret and enforce HTTPS.

Salesforce token parsing switches on global sharing flag despite fetching Salesforce directly

`parseRefreshTokenResponse(accessTokenJson, salesforceTokenSchema)` chooses the minimal schema whenever `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is set, even though this method always calls `login.salesforce.com` directly and never uses `refreshOAuthTokens`. Enabling credential sharing therefore makes Salesforce token parsing drop required fields such as `instance_url`, `id`, `issued_at`, `signature`, `scope`, and `token_type`; the stored DB key becomes incomplete and future connections can break.

Credential sync can create duplicate credentials under concurrent requests

The handler does `findFirst` and then either `update` or `create` in separate queries. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app can both miss the existing row and insert duplicates. There is also no deterministic choice if multiple rows exist. Use a transaction plus a unique constraint/upsert keyed by `(userId, appId, type)`.

Sync update does not mark credential valid again

When updating an existing credential, only `key` is changed. If that credential was previously marked `invalid: true` (for example after an invalid_grant failure), it remains invalid after syncing fresh credentials and may be skipped by integrations. The update should set `invalid: false` to reflect the new source-of-truth credential.

Office 365 video sync refresh can overwrite stored credential with an incomplete token

When sync mode returns the documented generic payload (`access_token` plus expiry date), `responseBody.expires_in` is undefined, so `expiry_date` is set to `Date.now()` (immediately expired), and the whole `responseBody` is stored as the key. The existing `refresh_token`, `token_type`, `scope`, and `email` are not preserved, so later refreshes fail. This integration needs to merge the sync response into the existing credential instead of replacing it.

AES-256 key generation command yields 24 bytes, not 32

The comment says the key must be 32 bytes for AES-256 and suggests `openssl rand -base64 24`. Base64-decoding 24 input bytes yields a 24-byte key, not 32. Users following this instruction will configure an invalid/weak key. Suggest `openssl rand -base64 32` or `openssl rand -hex 32`.

No tests for credential sync webhook or token refresh helpers

The PR adds a security-sensitive webhook, encryption/decryption path, and shared OAuth refresh/parsing helpers used by many integrations. The checklist explicitly says no tests were added. Given the parser shape mismatches and data-loss issues, tests for success, invalid secret, malformed payload, existing/update, and sync vs local refresh would catch regressions.

By that point search.init may already have started its watch goroutine, and Init may have initialized the backend, so these resources leak. Cancel ctx and perform cleanup on this path.

Unbounded per-group queues remove backpressure and can exhaust memory

FixedQueuePool creates `queue.Queue()` without a maxsize, so each per-group queue is unbounded, and FixedQueuePool.submit uses a non-blocking `put`. Contrary to the class docstring's 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', there is no backpressure; memory and OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound, risking OOM and a stalled consumer. This contradicts the graceful drain implied by `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and can cause in-flight backlog to be dropped until the consumer is restarted. The shutdown flag should not be set before queue drain, or the worker should drain until queue.ShutDown before exiting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing cache re-check after acquiring write lock causes thundering herd and I/O under exclusive lock

After the initial RLock sees entryPointAssetsCache == nil, the function takes the write lock and immediately performs readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN without re-reading entryPointAssetsCache. Multiple goroutines that all observed nil will therefore serialize on the write lock and each recompute and overwrite the cache, while all other GetWebAssets callers are blocked. Add a second check for a non-nil cache after acquiring the write lock (or use singleflight) before doing I/O.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flaw: GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so the double-checked locking pattern is incomplete and goroutines that saw a nil cache recompute it.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent test for the race fix

The PR changes shared-state synchronization but adds no test that exercises GetWebAssets concurrently. A test invoking GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines (run under the race detector) would verify both that the cache assignment is race-free and that the cache population path behaves correctly under contention.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup logs successful batch operations at error level

The new batch cleanup code calls r.log.Error for every batch even when there is no error: see lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579. For example, after fetchIDs succeeds, line 534 logs 'Annotations to clean by time' with err=nil, and line 537 logs 'cleaned annotations by time' even when deleteByIDs returns nil. These calls happen for no-op batches with zero IDs and can include large 'ids' slices up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (e.g. 32767). This floods logs with error-level events during normal cleanup, can trigger log-based alerts, and is misleading. Use Debug/Info for successful batch progress and avoid logging full ID slices at Error level.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: Error log level is used for non-error debugging and progress information, which pollutes the logs. Both suggest switching to Debug or Info instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded with the storage metric

The async legacy `DeleteCollection` result is recorded with `recordStorageDuration` and `startLegacy`. It should use `recordLegacyDuration`. As written, legacy successes and failures are attributed to storage metrics, corrupting both metric sets.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag swapped legacy/storage duration metric functions in DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection. The golden points to the storage failure path calling recordLegacyDuration, while the candidate points to the legacy path calling recordStorageDuration. The specific code path may differ, but the underlying bug is the same metric mix-up in the same method.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name as the metric kind label

This line passes `name` as the kind argument to `recordStorageDuration`, while other calls pass `options.Kind`. `name` is a user-controlled object name, so every deleted object creates a new Prometheus label value. This causes unbounded cardinality in the mode 3 storage metrics and can make metrics expensive or unusable. It should pass `options.Kind`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: the Delete call passes name instead of options.Kind to the metrics recording function, unlike the other methods. The candidate also explains the cardinality impact.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled after return

The goroutine at this line wraps the incoming request context with a 10s timeout and then performs Legacy.Create. The same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 108, 134, 161). In Kubernetes API server storage, the context passed to the storage method is typically canceled when the HTTP handler returns. Since this method returns immediately after launching the goroutine, the legacy backup write frequently starts with an already canceled context and is aborted, so mode 3 does not reliably keep legacy storage as a safe backup. Detach from the request lifecycle, for example with context.WithoutCancel/context.Background, before applying the timeout.

Legacy update reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object written to unified storage

This line passes the same `objInfo` that was already consumed by `d.Storage.Update` to `d.Legacy.Update`. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` may be single-use or may compute the new object against the old object in the target store; because legacy may have a different old object than unified storage, legacy can produce a different object or fail. The previous implementation wrapped the final object returned by storage in `updateWrapper` for the legacy update. The async legacy update should use the object returned by `d.Storage.Update`, or a wrapper that returns that object, rather than the original `objInfo`.

Storage create/update errors are recorded as legacy durations

On a `Storage.Create` error, the code records `recordLegacyDuration` with the storage start time even though no legacy call was made. The same mistake is present in `Update` at line 129. These should be `recordStorageDuration`. As written, storage failure metrics are underreported and legacy duration metrics are polluted with storage call durations.

Mode 3 integration tests immediately assert legacy consistency despite async legacy writes

The new mode 3 subtests run `doPlaylistTests`, which after k8s Create/Update immediately calls the legacy API and asserts that the change is present (for example the legacy list check and `getFromBothAPIs`). Mode 3 now writes to legacy asynchronously after the unified storage write returns, so these checks race with the legacy-write goroutine and can fail intermittently in CI. The tests should poll or wait for legacy convergence, or use a mode-specific expectation for async propagation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

Add `key={key}` to this branch.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say GrafanaRuleListItem is rendered in a list without a React key prop, which can cause reconciliation issues when the list changes. They describe the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

Silence menu item is shown but clicking it does nothing when only promRule is available

In the new prom-only rule list, RuleActionsButtons receives no `rule`/rulerRule. AlertRuleMenu shows the Silence item because `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` can report it as supported and allowed, and clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true. However this render condition requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`; with `rule` undefined it is false, so `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` is never rendered and the user-visible action is a dead click. Either hide/disable the Silence item when no ruler rule is available or make the drawer work from the prom rule.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug. RuleActionsButtons gets only promRule, and the Silence menu item is enabled through the Grafana prom abilities. Clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer, but the drawer only renders when a ruler rule exists, so nothing visible happens.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable in CombinedRule ability checks

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (still used by `useAlertRuleAbility` and `useAlertRuleAbilities`) now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false`. The previous `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` implementation computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and used it to make Update, Delete, Pause, and Restore unsupported for federated rule groups. After this change, CombinedRule callers can report those actions as supported for federated rules when the user has ordinary permissions, so the UI may expose edit/delete actions that are disallowed for federated rules.

Delete action is hidden for prom-only Grafana rules even when canDelete is true

The new alert list view passes `promRule` but no `rulerRule`. `canDelete` can be true via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, but the Delete menu item is guarded by both `canDelete` and `rulerRule`. Since `rulerRule` is undefined in the prom-only list, users with delete permission no longer see Delete for Grafana rules. `RuleActionsButtons` already builds a valid identifier from `promRule`, so this guard should be updated or the removal should be intentional and documented.

Pause action is never shown for prom-only Grafana rules despite canPause

`canPause` is computed using either rulerRule or Grafana prom rule abilities, and can be true in the new prom-only list. However the Pause menu item is additionally guarded by `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. With no rulerRule, the Pause item never renders, so the newly added `grafanaPauseAbility` is ineffective and pause access disappears from the alert list view.

Rule view link no longer preserves returnTo navigation

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` implementation used `createReturnTo()` and passed `{ returnTo }` to `createRelativeUrl` when building the rule view href. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` builds the same href without `returnTo`, so navigating from the rule list to the rule view no longer carries the return location and in-app back/return behavior can be regressed. If this is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise the `returnTo` query should be retained.

Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting bypasses the $__range split guard

The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` runs before `querySupportsSplitting`. `querySupportsSplitting` is designed to reject queries containing `$__range`/`$__range_ms` via `isQueryWithRangeVariable`, with a comment explaining these queries must not be split because the range variable would be interpreted relative to the split sub-range and produce an incorrect result. Since `applyTemplateVariables` replaces `$__range`/`$__range_ms`, the check on the interpolated expr no longer sees them and will allow time-splitting of those queries. The range-variable check should be performed on the pre-interpolated expression or otherwise preserve the raw expression for this guard.

Shard splitting applies template variables twice per query

`runShardSplitQuery` now interpolates every target with `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` at line 52. Later, `splitQueriesByStreamShard` sends each shard sub-request through `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which now also applies `applyTemplateVariables` to each target. Each query is interpolated again for every shard/time sub-request; the test change even asserts `applyTemplateVariables` is called five times for a single target. If variable replacement is not idempotent (for example, a variable value contains `$` or template-variable syntax), the second pass can change the query incorrectly. One of the two layers should avoid re-interpolating already-interpolated targets.

Queries can become empty after interpolation but are not re-filtered

The target pipe filters `query.expr` before `applyTemplateVariables`. When a non-empty template expression such as `$var` resolves to an empty string, the query remains in `queries` and proceeds through partitioning. Since the interpolated empty expr is not a logs query, it is treated as a metric query and sent to Loki with `expr: ''`. Reorder the pipe to interpolate first and then `.filter((query) => query.expr)` so queries whose value is empty are skipped.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, performs an upsert. There is no transaction, lock, or database-enforced cap around these two operations. Concurrent requests from different devices can all observe a count below the limit and then insert, so the configured device limit can be exceeded under normal concurrent anonymous traffic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: the device count check and the insert are not atomic, so concurrent requests can push the device count past the limit. Both suggest a transaction or lock as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RowsAffected == 0 can incorrectly reject existing devices on MySQL

updateDevice treats RowsAffected() == 0 as proof that no existing device was updated and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL default behavior, the affected-row count for UPDATE is the number of rows changed, not rows matched. An existing device row whose client_ip, user_agent, and updated_at already equal the supplied values can produce 0 affected rows and be rejected incorrectly. Use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS, a follow-up existence check, or otherwise distinguish 'updated an existing row' from 'no matching row'.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the same code: updateDevice mapping RowsAffected()==0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached. The golden says zero rows means the device is missing or outside the time window, not that a limit was hit. The candidate's main point is a MySQL quirk where unchanged rows report 0 affected. It does still say that 0 rows is wrongly treated as limit-reached and that 'no matching row' needs to be told apart from an update. That overlaps with the golden's semantic error, though the emphasis differs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit rejection is bypassable by retrying with the same device ID

In tagDeviceUI the local cache entry is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice. When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry remains. TagDevice propagates the error so the first anonymous authentication request fails, but any subsequent request with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id on the same instance within the 29-minute local-cache TTL sees the cached key and returns nil without touching the store. Anonymous.Authenticate then succeeds, so a client can bypass the configured device limit simply by retrying.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice, so when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned the entry remains and later requests bypass the device limit for the 29-minute TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
Clients can bypass the device limit by omitting the device ID header

TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is empty. Since Anonymous.Authenticate now only rejects when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, an anonymous request that omits this header is never counted and always proceeds even when the configured limit has been reached. If the device limit is intended to be enforced, missing or empty device IDs should not silently skip enforcement.

Anonymous authentication now blocks on synchronous device-store writes

Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously before returning an identity. On a local-cache miss, TagDevice performs a database count when the limit is enabled and an insert/update upsert for each new device, and again after the 29-minute local-cache TTL. Previously this work ran in a background goroutine with a timeout and did not delay login. This adds database latency and database-availability risk to the anonymous authentication path.

Authn client is coupled to the anonstore storage package for a sentinel error

Authenticate imports pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore and uses errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached). This couples the authentication client to a concrete database-store implementation. The sentinel error should be part of the anonymous service contract or a shared service package so alternate anonymous.Service implementations can signal the same condition without importing storage internals.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are loaded only for controller requests

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only called from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. `I18n.translate` in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb` lazy-loads only the current locale via `load_locale(config.locale)`, so translations performed outside controller actions (for example mailers, background jobs, or rake tasks) with a non-default locale will not have the site-default or `:en` YAML loaded before fallback lookup runs. A missing key in the current locale can then fail or produce an I18n missing-translation error instead of falling back. The fallback preloading must happen wherever `I18n.locale` is set, or `translate` should load the fallback chain itself.

Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain

The cached translation key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. With the new fallback chain `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]`, a translation that is missing in the requested locale can be resolved from a fallback locale and then cached under the requested locale. If `SiteSetting.default_locale` changes at runtime, the same key and locale would need a different fallback resolution, but the old cached value is still returned until `I18n.reload!` clears the cache. This can serve stale translations after an admin changes the default locale. Include the fallback chain in the cache key or invalidate the translation cache when the default locale changes.

No tests cover the new fallback behavior

This PR introduces a custom fallback order, loads fallbacks and pluralization in a new initializer, removes environment-specific fallback flags, and adds `ensure_loaded!` wiring, but no specs are added. The behavior should be tested: anonymous users use the site default, logged-in users fall back in the expected order, fallback locale YAMLs are actually loaded, and non-controller translation paths do not regress. Without tests, this lazy-loading/fallback interaction is easy to break.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request logs lose traceID

The previous `logRequest` appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to the request completion log. This change removes that field and the `tracing` import. The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname; it does not add a trace ID. Unless some unchanged middleware already injects traceID as a contextual log attribute, `Plugin Request Completed` entries will no longer contain a trace ID, breaking log-to-trace correlation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. The traceID logging from tracing.TraceIDFromContext was removed from the logger middleware along with the tracing import. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add traceID, so plugin request logs no longer carry it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext drops the logger whose logs tests inspect

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning `f` or a logger that shares `f`'s `Logs` fields. Since `LoggerMiddleware` now logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, any test that passes a `*TestLogger` and then asserts on the original logger's `InfoLogs`/`ErrorLogs` will observe zero calls because the actual log is written to a brand-new `TestLogger`. The fake should preserve the same test logger or share its log counters/fields.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: TestLogger.FromContext returns NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver f. As a result, logs are recorded on a new instance and test assertions against the original logger fail.

false_positives.candidate:
LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware

`LoggerMiddleware` no longer includes pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, or dsUID in its own log params. It now calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` and expects those fields to already be present in the context. Production middleware ordering in `CreateMiddlewares` inserts `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` before it, so the production path gets those fields. However `NewLoggerMiddleware` is exported and can be used independently; any caller that builds a middleware stack without the new contextual middleware will get request logs with those fields silently missing. This hidden ordering dependency should be documented, enforced, or avoided by keeping the fields inside `LoggerMiddleware`.

Adding FromContext to Logger is a source-breaking interface change

The exported `log.Logger` interface now requires `FromContext(context.Context) Logger`. Any existing implementation outside this package, including external/enterprise code, will no longer satisfy the interface and will fail to compile until it adds the method. If `pkg/plugins/log` is consumed as an API, this should be introduced as an optional interface or with a compatibility/deprecation path.

Exported InstrumentationMiddleware symbols removed without compatibility aliases

This renames the exported `InstrumentationMiddleware` type and `NewInstrumentationMiddleware` constructor to `MetricsMiddleware` and `NewMetricsMiddleware`. Because `pkg/services/pluginsintegration/clientmiddleware` is not an `internal` package, downstream importers such as enterprise or external code will fail to compile after upgrading. If the package is public API, keep deprecated alias symbols during the transition or coordinate the breaking change explicitly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy embeddable hosts are inserted without normalization and will not match the new host check

This migration inserts each `h` verbatim into `embeddable_hosts.host`, but `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?`/`record_for_host` parses the incoming referer and compares only `uri.host` to the stored `lower(host)`. true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problem: the migration inserts legacy hosts without normalization, which may include a scheme or path. The new lookup compares only the bare host, so migrated entries won't match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

Category and embeddable host fabricator contents were swapped

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now defines `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category` definitions. true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: the contents of the category and embeddable host fabricator files were swapped, which can cause fabricator errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Hosts saved with a port can never match

The host format validation allows an optional `:port` (line 2), and `before_validation` does not strip it. However `record_for_host` compares only `uri.host` to the stored `lower(host)`, ignoring `uri.port`. A host entered as `example.com:8080` will therefore never match `http://example.com:8080`. false_positives.candidate:
Request-reschedule workflow reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async and are called in a `forEach` without being awaited. The old code collected and awaited `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany` promises. The mutation continues to send the reschedule request and returns; in a serverless environment the process can be frozen before the deferred `cancelled = true` update is written. The old workflow reminders can then still fire after the booking was put into the reschedule path.

Workflow update cancels reminders without awaiting DB writes

`remindersToDelete.flat().forEach(...)` calls the async managers without awaiting them, and the later `userWorkflow.steps.map(async (oldStep) => ...)` promises are also never awaited. The mutation subsequently updates the workflow and returns, so email/SMS cancellation calls and related DB deletes/updates can still be in flight. A cancelled reminder may be re-created or the old reminder may remain uncancelled, allowing emails/SMS from a disabled or edited workflow to be sent after the update completes.

One failed SendGrid cancellation prevents deletion of already-cancelled rows

The loop awaits each `client.request` sequentially and only afterwards calls `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)`. If any later SendGrid request throws, the `catch` runs before the delete promises are awaited, so rows for which cancellation already succeeded are not deleted. They remain `cancelled = true` and are retried on the next cron run, generating duplicate SendGrid cancellation requests and keeping stale rows until a run with no cancellation failures. The delete should be awaited immediately after a successful cancellation or the final `Promise.all` should run in a `finally`.

Paid bookings return before scheduled workflow reminders are cancelled

When `bookingToDelete.paid` is true, the handler refunds the payment, marks the booking REJECTED, and returns at this line. This is before the block at lines 484-493 that cancels scheduled workflow reminders. As a result, paid/rejected bookings with scheduled workflow reminders will still have those reminder emails/SMS sent after cancellation. This path is not covered by the PR's cancellation fix.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklisted email comparison is case-sensitive

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased before comparison, but incoming `guest` values are not normalized. An email such as `Blocked@example.com` can bypass a blacklist entry of `blocked@example.com` and be added to the booking. Normalize incoming guests with `.toLowerCase()` before comparing, or better normalize in the schema/handler before all validation.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug: the blacklist is lowercased but the guest input is not, so uppercase emails bypass the blacklist.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. This means a team admin who is not an owner, or an owner who is not an admin, is denied. The variable name and intended behavior indicate an OR condition; use `||` or separate the two permission checks.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: the team admin/owner permission check uses && where it should use ||, so a user who is only an admin or only an owner gets denied.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Incoming duplicate guests are not deduplicated server-side

`uniqueGuests` filters incoming guests only against existing `booking.attendees` and the blacklist; it does not deduplicate the incoming `guests` array. The server schema `z.array(z.string().email())` does not enforce uniqueness, so a caller can pass the same email twice with different casing and `createMany` will insert duplicate attendee records for the same booking, causing duplicate calendar invites and inconsistent attendee data. Deduplicate case-insensitively on the server before insertion.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. uniqueGuests filters only against existing attendees and the blacklist, and never deduplicates the incoming list itself, so createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows. The candidate's added case-insensitivity detail is an extension of that point, not a different issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type email disable settings

Other email helpers in this file respect `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` and `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`, but `sendAddGuestsEmails` sends organizer and attendee emails unconditionally. Users who disabled standard host or attendee emails for an event type will still receive these add-guests notifications, violating their email preferences. Pass `eventTypeMetadata` to this function and check the relevant disable flags before sending.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same problem: sendAddGuestsEmails does not check the event type metadata's email-disable flags, so hosts and attendees can still get emails after standard emails were disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add guests to a booking

The handler grants permission to any user whose email appears in `booking.attendees` via `isAttendee`. This exposes the tRPC mutation to every attendee, allowing them to add arbitrary emails to the booking without organizer approval. New attendees may receive calendar invitations and meeting details. Unless attendee self-service is an explicit requirement, restrict this mutation to the organizer or team admins/owners.

Calendar update uses caller credentials instead of organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` returns the authenticated caller's credentials, but the event belongs to `booking.user` (the organizer). The `EventManager` is then pointed at the organizer's destination calendar via `evt.destinationCalendar`. If the caller is not the organizer, this mismatch can make `updateCalendarAttendees` fail or attempt to update the wrong account's calendar. Use the booking organizer's credentials (e.g., `booking.user.credentials`) or load credentials for the organizer.

No tests cover the new addGuests mutation

This new tRPC mutation introduces authorization rules, email blacklisting, deduplication concerns, and external calendar/email side effects, but no tests are added. Missing coverage makes it easy for permission bypasses and duplicate-handling regressions to go unnoticed. Add tests for authorized and unauthorized callers, duplicate/blacklisted emails, and missing bookings.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code single-use consumption is not atomic

The code reads `user.backupCodes`, validates the submitted code with `indexOf`, and then later writes the whole array back with the matched index set to `null`. There is no transaction or conditional update. Two concurrent requests using the same backup code can both pass validation before either write happens, so both sessions are authorized. Requests using different backup codes can also lose updates because each writes a stale array, leaving an already-used code active. The one-time-code guarantee should be enforced with an atomic/conditional update.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: concurrent requests with the same backup code can both pass validation before the write-back, so a single-use code gets accepted more than once.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code login bypasses password when a totpCode is also supplied

The password verification block at line 121 only runs when `credentials.totpCode` is falsy. The new backup-code branch at line 131 is chosen whenever `credentials.backupCode` is present, and it never verifies the password itself. A caller can therefore authenticate with `email`, a valid `backupCode`, and any non-empty `totpCode` (for example `000000`): the truthy `totpCode` skips password verification, then the backup code is validated and authorize returns the user. A stolen/leaked backup code alone becomes sufficient to sign in, defeating two-factor protection.

First 2FA enable test does not close the new backup-code screen before asserting state

`handleEnable` now leaves the modal on the new `DisplayBackupCodes` screen and does not call `onEnable` until the `backup-codes-close` button is clicked. This test enters the OTP and immediately asserts the two-factor switch is checked, so it checks state before the parent is notified/refetched. The second test was updated to click `backup-codes-close` and assert `data-state="checked"`; this test should do the same. As written it either fails or passes due to the already-noted unreliable `isChecked()` assertion.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google updateEvent fallback calendar lookup always misses

When `externalCalendarId` is falsy, the fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`, which compares each calendar's externalId against null/undefined and returns undefined. `calendar.events.update` is then called with an undefined calendarId instead of the previous behavior of using `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. The same broken pattern appears in `deleteEvent` around line 317. Legacy bookings or references without `externalCalendarId` will fail to update/delete Google Calendar events.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same flawed lookup, `destinationCalendar.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)`, which is circular and cannot produce a useful result. The golden comment frames it for the case where externalCalendarId is provided. The candidate frames it for the falsy case, where the find returns undefined. The line and the bug are the same: the lookup logic is wrong and should use something like credentialId instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Organization creation slug condition is inverted

The diff changes `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, and similarly changes `requestedSlug` in the metadata. This is the opposite of the previous logic and is unrelated to the destinationCalendar change. With billing disabled, new organizations no longer receive a slug, likely breaking org creation/URLs; with billing enabled, slug is now set when it was previously withheld in favor of requestedSlug. Revert this condition unless there is a separate intentional billing change.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the slug condition on IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED was inverted. The result is that slug is set when billing is enabled and missing when it is disabled. The candidate's wording about requestedSlug differs slightly, but it points to the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Office365 createEvent always targets the first destination calendar

Even though EventManager now iterates all destination calendars and calls `createEvent` once per credential, Office365 still destructures only the first element of `event.destinationCalendar` and ignores the supplied credentialId. For a collective event with multiple hosts, every Office365 invocation targets the same first host calendar, causing duplicate events in that calendar and no event in the other hosts' Office365 calendars. The service must select the destination whose credentialId matches the current credential, similar to GoogleCalendarService. LarkCalendarService and BaseCalendarService have the same first-element-only behavior.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment is about an interface signature mismatch: implementations declare createEvent(event) without the credentialId parameter. The candidate is about runtime behavior: the services ignore credentialId and always use the first destination calendar. The two overlap, since both involve Lark and Office365 not using credentialId. However, the candidate does not flag the missing parameter in the method signature as an interface contract violation. It is related but frames a different issue (a logic bug versus a signature contract). Under a loose reading, ignoring the supplied credentialId implies the parameter is missing, so this is a partial match.

false_positives.candidate:
Google Meet fallback crashes when destinationCalendar is empty

`evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` produces an empty array when no destination calendar is set, so `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is undefined. The next line dereferences `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`, throwing a TypeError before the intended fallback to Daily can run. Previously `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration` was safely undefined. Use optional chaining, e.g. `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

updateLocation creates booking references without externalCalendarId or credentialId

`referencesToCreate` now reads `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` does not return either field (unlike `createEvent`). After editing a location, the newly created calendar `BookingReference` rows will have null `externalCalendarId` and null `credentialId`. Later cancellation/reschedule/update logic cannot identify the external calendar or credential, so it may target the wrong calendar or fail to delete/update the right event. Either `updateEvent` should return these fields, or `updateLocation` should derive them from the calendar reference being updated.

Google Meet description patch uses undefined calendarId when no selected calendar

`calendar.events.insert` uses `selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the subsequent `calendar.events.patch` uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without that fallback. When no destination in the array matches the current credentialId, `selectedCalendar` is undefined; the insert proceeds against primary, but the patch that adds the hangout link fails because the calendarId is undefined. Use the same fallback in both calls.

Team destination calendars are dropped when organizer has no destinationCalendar

`evt.destinationCalendar` is initialized to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer user has a destination calendar. The team calendars are then added with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`, which is a no-op on null. If the organizer has no destination calendar but the other collective hosts do, all collected `teamDestinationCalendars` are lost and EventManager falls back to the organizer's first connected calendar rather than creating events in the hosts' selected calendars. Initialize `evt.destinationCalendar` to an array before pushing or assign the combined array explicitly.

Confirmed collective bookings only schedule the first destination calendar

When a booking requiring confirmation is later confirmed, this handler rebuilds `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` from `booking.destinationCalendar` (a single Prisma relation) or the confirming user's default. The multi-host `teamDestinationCalendars` assembled at initial booking time are not persisted or reconstructed here. `handleConfirmation`/EventManager therefore creates calendar events only for the first destination, not for all hosts of a collective event.

Paid collective bookings schedule only the first destination calendar

Both `getBooking` and `handlePaymentSuccess` build `evt.destinationCalendar` from the booking's single `destinationCalendar` or the user default. For a paid collective event, the multi-host destination calendars assembled in `handleNewBooking` are not available here and are not stored on the booking. When payment succeeds and `EventManager.create` runs, only the first/primary calendar receives the event; other hosts are not scheduled. The same issue exists in `paypal-webhook.ts`.

Recurring cancellation still deletes only one organizer calendar reference

Inside the new loop over `bookingCalendarReference`, the recurring/allRemaining branch ignores the current reference's `credentialId` and instead maps over `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` (the organizer's own credentials). For each updated booking it then calls `references.find(...)`, which returns only the first calendar reference. For a collective recurring booking with multiple host calendars, this repeats deletion of the first organizer-visible event and never deletes events belonging to the other host references. It should iterate all calendar references and use each reference's credential/externalCalendarId.

All Google calendar events use the first destination as organizer

`mainHostDestinationCalendar` is always the first element of `event.destinationCalendar`, and its externalId is used as the organizer email for every create/update invocation. When EventManager iterates the other host destination calendars with different credentialIds, the event is inserted into another host's calendar but the organizer attendee is still set to the first host's externalId. This can set the wrong organizer/permissions or cause Google to reject the event. The organizer email should correspond to the destination/credential being processed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach async callbacks are not awaited, so cancellation errors are lost

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` starts an async callback for each reference but `forEach` discards the returned promise. The surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections after the callback suspends, so a failed `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled rejection and the function returns before external calendar/video cancellation is known to have completed. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: forEach with async callbacks for calendar and video deletions is not awaited. This produces unhandled rejections that the surrounding try/catch cannot catch, and the work may not finish before the function returns. Both propose the same fixes, Promise.all with map or a for...of loop.

false_positives.candidate:
requestReschedule does not await async calendar/video cancellation callbacks

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` discards the promise returned by each async callback. The mutation continues immediately to send reschedule emails and webhooks, so external calendar/video cancellation for the old booking may still be running, and any rejection from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled rejection. Convert this to `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop.

Recurring cancellation starts unawaited async callbacks and `apiDeletes` is captured too early

In the recurring cancellation branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` does not await the callbacks. Each callback suspends at `await getCalendar`, so the later `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` captures `apiDeletes` before these callbacks resume and push their calendar deletions. As a result, recurring calendar events are not deleted/cancelled before booking references and attendees are removed and cancellation emails are sent. Use `await Promise.all(credentials.map(async (credential) => { ... }))` instead of `forEach`.
